newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian minister seeks cheaper energy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian minister seeks cheaper energy.

text.p: Russia's energy minister called for lower fuel prices to help domestic firms in an interview published on Thursday, but said nothing about how to finance the move or what it would do for a cash-strapped budget.

"The fuel and energy ministry should conduct tariff policies in such a way that prices of the fuel and energy complex stimulate economic growth," Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov told Nezavisimaya Gazeta in an interview.
"Without question the general price level of all fuel and energy resources needs to be decreased." He made clear he was talking about lower prices for industry not for domestic consumers.

But Western economists said lower energy prices would either cut company profits or -- if accompanied by big new subsidies -- would boost government spending. Both could hurt government plans to cut the budget deficit.
Lower prices also meant it would be harder to attract much-needed investment to the energy sector, they said.
"I would have thought that the argument of lower energy prices was dead and buried a year or so ago," said World Bank chief Moscow economist Vladimir Konovalov.

"We have given the government a lot of marks for moving towards world prices. I would have thought that an energy minister's interests would be energy, not worrying about lumbering old factories which want cheap power."
Heavily subsidised energy was a trademark of the Soviet economic system and homes and factories were designed with little regard for how to keep electricity or heating costs low.
Soviet-made cars and aeroplanes use more fuel than their Western equivalents, families open windows in mid-winter to keep overheated apartments cool and factories pay scant regard to energy costs.
But Russian companies have struggled to compete with a market economy and industrial output has virtually halved since the Soviet Union fell apart.
Many ministers, praising steep falls in monthly inflation rates as a sign that the longed-for stabilisation has finally arrived, say Russia must now go for economic growth.
Rodionov said low energy and energy transport prices were needed to help domestic firms.
"Prices for energy transport should be at a level to allow competitiveness with other countries," he said.
Rodionov, previously the head of a St Petersburg subsidiary of national gas monopoly Gazprom, was appointed in August and is little known in the West.
Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital in Moscow, there were better ways to help companies than by lowering energy prices.
"It is much more important for industry to make sure that the budget deficit stays low, that inflation stays low and the exchange rate remains stable," he said.

Russian consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in September, after a seasonally-influenced fall of 0.2 percent in August. The 1997 budget envisages a tight deficit of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, after 3.85 percent this year.
Parliament is due to start full hearings on the budget on October 11.
